utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beara. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I seem to have a technical difficulty with my headphones. I think it's okay, yes. Thank you. Mr. Beara, although you know -- may I know this very well, but I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal before you commence your evidence. That is, Rule 90(E). You may object to answering any question under this rule from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question; but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled under such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beara. Before we go on, I would like to counsel assisting Mr. Beara to introduce himself for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is John Ostojic. I'm here on behalf of Mr. Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. But, Mr. Robinson, I was informed before I entered the courtroom that Mr. Beara hasn't been informed that cross-examination of -- his cross-examination would be postponed after the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Well, I informed his counsel, and I don't know from there what communication they had. But Mr. Ostojic was informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Beara, in order for the Prosecutor to have some time to prepare for their cross-examination of you, the Chamber agreed with the arrangements that were made between the parties so that your cross-examination will be postponed after the recess. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that. I found out about that this morning. Mr. Ostojic told me about it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am waiting for the interpretation and I ask you also to pause between question and answer. Thank you for having come. We don't want anything to be lost in translation, so I am going to put a few questions to you in the English language, slowly, carefully, and they will be interpreted to you carefully.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for this being in English, but it is going to be interpreted properly. [In English] Can you tell us what positions you held during your military career?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: I graduated from the military naval academy in 1962, and then first I served on the 11th Split destroyer. Then I was in Ploce on minesweepers. I was a ship commander. After that unit of minesweepers was dissolved, I was in Brijuni in the Guards Naval Detachment. That is where I was admitted into the security service of the JNA. Then I served in Pula, in Split, in the counter-intelligence group, and then in Boka as chief of the security department of the 9th Naval Sector Kumbor. Then again in Split as a desk officer at the security department. Then assistant for security and staff affairs and assistant chief of security, and then assistant chief of security for the military naval sector for counter-intelligence. And ultimately, I was chief of the security department of the command of the military naval district. When - how do I put this? - when the tribal war started in Bosnia, I was in Belgrade. I was there because the military naval district no longer existed, and then they assigned me to the Army of Republika Srpska. Over there, I was first chief of the security department in the command of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. And then from 1995, I think, or maybe 1994, I can no longer remember, I was chief of administration -- well, it was changed, this formation, the establishment was somewhat changed. And I ended the war as chief of department, and I retired.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the witness. Could all other the microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't follow you. Could you repeat from where -- from 1994, where you were chief of administration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I came to the VRS in November 1992, 1991. Again, I don't know. And then I was chief of the security department at the security intelligence sector of the Main Staff of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska. And from 1994 or 1995, the establishment changed and it wasn't the security department anymore. It was the security administration. Then I was chief of that administration until I retired. Or that is to say, until the Main Staff was dissolved because then the General Staff was established, headed by General Pero something - I no longer remember his last name - who was in Bijeljina. Excuse me. I stayed in Crna Rijeka. We had built some facilities there, and the idea was that we make a vacation facility there for the wives and children of those who were killed during the war. And we built a multi-storey building, there was a kitchen, a dining area, and so on and so forth; however, this was not fully carried through. I actually left -- I retired, and I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Karadzic. The Chamber needs to rise for ten minutes. Court deputy, follow the Judges. --- Break taken at 9.16 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So please tell us, what was your position in the VRS in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: I think that I said that just now. I was chief of the security administration of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever inform me, either orally or in writing, that prisoners from Srebrenica would be, were being, or had been executed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I and my lawyer have received these questions earlier. Mr. Ostojic, my lawyer, counselled me that I invoke 90(E) with regard to this question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, would you like to make any observation in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just to confirm that, yes, indeed, we've discussed it, and Mr. Beara and both I and he would like to invoke 90(E) on this with respect to his testimony in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We would ask that the Trial Chamber compel Colonel Beara to answer this question and afford him the full protections of Rule 90(E), assuring him that testimony compelled in this way would not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against him for any offence other than false testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the Prosecution like to make an observation in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Only to note, Mr. President, that the reference to "subsequent prosecution" seems to ignore what is likely to be the genuine subject of the witness's focus and Mr. Ostojic's focus as well, and that is the current proceedings and the appeal. So on the record, it appears to be a bit misleading and I think that needed to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson mentioned, and I'm reading from the transcript, "the full protections of Rule 90(E), assuring him that testimony compelled in this way would not be used as evidence in the subsequent prosecution" or perhaps he meant "any subsequent prosecution," I was simply indicating that the use of the word "subsequent" in these circumstances seemed to ignore what was in fact the object of the witness's and his counsel's concern, and that is the current proceeding. I appreciate that the language is taken verbatim from the rule; nevertheless, the rule may not specifically have contemplated this situation. In any event, it seemed to create a potential area of misunderstanding and I raised it for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was quoting directly from the rule, but since the Appeals Chamber has decided in General Tolimir's case that no statements made by the witness would be used in their appeal proceedings, then that would also be applicable here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have nothing to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We -- as obviously we weren't the moving force behind calling this witness and given our other responsibilities, we have not undertaken an exhaustive investigation of the issues in law that may pertain to any questions that arise here, so we have nothing beyond the comments I just made at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise for 15 minutes. --- Break taken at 9.36 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will now rule on the witness's request to invoke Rule 90(E), not to respond to Mr. Karadzic's question as to the witness's informing the accused about the execution of prisoners in Srebrenica. The Chamber has considered the arguments of the parties and has decided to compel the witness to answer the question. The Chamber reminds the witness of the protection afforded to him by Rule 90(E), which was recently confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in the Tolimir case on the 13th of November, 2013. This protection means that the witness may be compelled to testify in this case due to the fact that any self-incrimination question elicited in this case -- proceedings cannot be directly or derivatively used against him in his own case. I said "cannot be directly or derivatively used." Yes. Mr. Beara, the Chamber is therefore instructing you to answer Mr. Karadzic's question. The Chamber now invites the parties and the counsel for witness to submit as to whether we should proceed in public or private session. Who shall I hear from first? Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We would ask to proceed in public session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the language used by the Chamber in reliance upon the decision of the Appeals Chamber, we think it's very clear that the matter must proceed in private session in order to maintain any level of control over the -- of access to those matters such that the assurance offered the witness can be complied with. The -- the language of the underlying rule explicitly, 90(E), refers to the use of evidence in subsequent proceedings. That presumably means by not only this institution but others. If such control is to be maintained and the cautionary language lent meaning, that means that it can't be distributed internationally from the outset for use by anyone. And that's separate from the issue of the relative meaning of derivative use versus direct use. So we think it's very clear and we should proceed in private session. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We take no position with respect to this issue of whether it should be private or public or open session, and we'll defer to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having considered the submissions, the Chamber considers it appropriate if we proceed in private session. The Chamber will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Beara, I take it you followed the proceedings. Shall I ask Mr. Karadzic to repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need. I understood it the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My lawyer and myself asked to be allowed to invoke 90(E) because we thought that the question was actually incriminating for myself. If I say that I didn't report to Mr. Karadzic, that would mean that I knew but I didn't inform him. However, if I told -- if I said that I didn't inform him, it would be the same. In other words, I knew but I kept it a secret from him. In the course of the trial against my group, we found a document where it says clear that Mr. Karadzic should have been informed as to what was going on in Srebrenica and around it. If necessary, I can give you the name or the number of the document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could I pose the question again? I didn't get the answer, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please ask your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the question is: Did you ever inform me either orally or in writing that prisoners from Srebrenica would be, were being, or had been executed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the answer is the same. How could I inform you. Pursuant to the rules of subordination, that was not possible. If I had known about it and if I didn't inform you, as I have already told you, why didn't I? If I had known, I could not have informed you because pursuant to the rules of subordination, I was not linked to you in any way. But you knew it. Why are you asking me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Just to have answers of my five questions and then we'll go. Please. Next question would be: Did we ever speak during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I know that I did see you from time to time. Whether we spoke or not, again, we are talking about subordination. I was far from you and you were even further away from me. I don't think that we spoke. I did see you and I don't mean on TV, I saw you in person. Now, as to whether you saw me or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did -- during the war, did you ever author or read any VRS document that indicated that prisoners from Srebrenica would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. I'm sorry to interrupt you. But I wonder whether we have to repeat these questions in private session. Whenever he invokes Rule 90(E), we go into private session. Can I hear from the parties or Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We will, just so you know, with respect to question number five, I believe invoke Rule 90(E). But with respect to the prior question that was asked, we did not and that's why we didn't stand. The question for number five has not yet been completed, but I believe from my understanding with Mr. Beara that we would invoke Rule 90(E) for the fifth question as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I don't know if that was a -- that resolved the Court's concerns, but when the Court raised it, it seemed to me it was raising a very obvious procedural point. We would expect to be in open session for questions to be asked, then -- then the witness invokes or doesn't invoke, and then depending on that circumstance we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Given the emphasis by the Defence in particular on the need for openness, but irrespective of that, just in terms of the way one would normally expect to proceed, I think the Court's suggestion was in keeping with conventional expectations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So should we go into open session and repeat with question number four and go on with number five? Unless there is any objection, we'll go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we ever speak during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: As I've already said, we did see each other or, rather, I saw you, but I don't think that we ever spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war, did you ever author or read any VRS document that indicated that prisoners from Srebrenica would be, were being, or had been executed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA BEARA
utterances.text: Is this a question for 90(E)? Would that fall under that rule? Would the same thing apply as for the previous questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Beara, likewise, the Chamber is compelling you to answer the question with the full protection as provided in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understand that. A brief answer would be no. If any such document had been produced, it would have surfaced by now. I believe that the Prosecutor has obtained all sorts of papers, documents, orders, plans, and so on and so forth. Therefore, my answer is this: I never authored an order of that kind, nor did I ever see such an order in a written form. It is also true that nobody ever orally ordered me any such thing, nor did I hear anybody order anybody else any such thing. So this would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would like to ask that the answers of the matters that have been heard in private session be reclassified as public in light of the witness's answers. There is nothing his answers that would remotely incriminate him and therefore subject him to any kind of foreign prosecution, and as a result, I believe that it's in the interest of justice that these proceedings be entirely public. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger or Ms. Pack, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, only to note that -- that Mr. Robinson puts that possible issue before us. I think given the matters involved, at a minimum, we wouldn't want to jump to the conclusion that no one would be interested in or could possibly use it. I would think that would be a determination that would only be made by the Chamber with absolute certainty and that would certainly require a much closer scrutiny of the record than we have been able to do thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, further to that, Mr. Tieger, isn't this a matter to be reconsidered at the conclusion of any cross-examination as to his answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a very good point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We have nothing to add on the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider this issue when the cross-examination will have been over. But do we have any clue when we'll have the cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have agreed on the date of the 22nd of January for the cross-examination if that is suitable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 22nd. Very well. Then we'll continue with the cross-examination of Mr. Beara on the 22nd. Mr. Beara, on behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will have a break for about -- is 20 minutes sufficient for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see how it evolves. We'll have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the Prosecution, to Mr. Karadzic and his Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the record, I note the presence of Mr. Ostojic to assist Mr. Stakic. Although the witness is present, I'd like to deal with three matters. Please bear with us, Mr. Stakic, for a moment. The Chamber will first turn to the accused's "Precautionary Rule 94 bis Notice: Marko Sladojevic," filed yesterday and on which the Chamber heard oral submissions yesterday. The Chamber finds it unnecessary to wait till the English translation will be completed. In conclusion, the Chamber does not agree that Mr. Sladojevic should be compared to Prosecution witnesses Jean-Rene Ruez and Dean Manning who both participated on the ground and in investigations and exhumations and who could testify as fact witnesses as to what they saw at the time and the process through which the Prosecution evidence was collected. The Chamber also recalls that Mrs. Hanson and Mr. Nielsen testified as expert witnesses, and therefore the comparison with Mr. Sladojevic is inadequate. Furthermore, the Chamber is of the view that Mr. Sladojevic, in his report, seemed to have conducted the kind of analysis which is typically addressed by parties in their final briefs or closing arguments. The Chamber would not be assisted at all by allowing this type of compilation from a team member of one of the parties to be admitted on the record. The Chamber will therefore not allow Mr. Sladojevic to be heard as a witness in these proceedings and will not admit his study entitled, and I quote, "Thus Spoke Radovan Karadzic" into evidence. Second, the Chamber is seized of the accused's request for oral testimony during sentencing case, also filed yesterday. In this request, the accused asked that the Chamber receive oral testimony during the sentencing phase of his case and that such evidence be heard upon the conclusion of any witnesses called by the Chamber. The Chamber recalls that during the Status Conference of 3rd of September, 2012, it reminded the Defence that the Defence 65 ter witness list should identify all the witnesses it intended to call, including sentencing witnesses. In its, I quote, "Decision on Time Allocated to the Accused for the Presentation of his Case," issued on the 19th of September, 2012, the Chamber made it clear that the 300 hours initially granted to him would be for the direct examination and re-examination of all of his witnesses. This remains the Chamber's position and no additional time will be granted to the accused to present oral evidence related to sentencing. It is for the accused to decide how to spend the remainder of his time, and should he decide to spend all or some of his time on sentencing matters, the Chamber would not interfere with that decision as long as it considers the evidence to be of relevance. However, any such sentencing-related evidence should be presented before the end of Defence case and within the 325 hours allocated to the accused. Third, the Chamber will issue its oral ruling on the "Mladic Motion for Access to Trial Audio Recordings in Karadzic Case," filed confidentially by the Mladic Defence on the 16th of December, 2013. In this motion, the Mladic Defence requests access to all trial audio recordings from the Karadzic case, noting that it has already been granted access to closed and private session trial transcript from this case. The Chamber notes that on the 16th of December, 2013, the accused's legal advisor informed the Chamber and the parties via e-mail that he would not be filing a response to this motion. The Chamber has not heard from the Prosecution or the Registry but is of the view that it can issue this oral decision nevertheless, particularly given the submission in paragraph 6 of the motion in which the Mladic Defence recounts the discussion it has had with the Registry on this issue. As pointed out by the Mladic Defence, the Chamber recalls that, on the 8th of November, 2012, it issued a decision allowing Mladic - pursuant to Rules 54, 70, and 75 - access to all closed and private session transcripts from this case which are not subject to Rule 70 or delayed disclosure and which are produced in the pre-trial and trial proceedings. Accordingly, given the broad access that Mladic Defence already has to confidential information from this case, the Chamber will grant the request outlined in the motion pursuant to the same Rules. The Chamber reminds the Mladic Defence, the parties in this case, and the Registry, that those parts of paragraph 20 of the access decision of the 8th of November, 2012, which apply to the transcripts of the proceedings, shall also apply, mutatis mutandis, to the audio recordings. Final, the Chamber notes that the Mladic Defence filed this motion confidentially. The Chamber could discern no reason on the face of the motion for its confidential status. It therefore orders the Registry to reclassify it as public. The Registry is requested to communicate this decision to the Mladic Defence. Having said that, I would like Mr. Karadzic to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I still need to do is read a short summary of your statement, and then I will probably hand you over to the Prosecutor. [In English] Dr. Milomir Stakic appeared on the SDS list for the first multi-party elections in BH as an independent candidate. On 18th of November, 1990, he was elected deputy in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, and on the 4th of January, 1991, he was appointed vice-president of the Assembly. He held the posts of president of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Prijedor municipality, president of the Prijedor municipality, and president of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality. After the multi-party elections of BH in 1990, the authorities in Prijedor were constituted from members of the SDA, SDS, and HDZ, in accordance with an agreement on the republican revel. On 4th of January, 1991, the new multi-party Assembly of the municipality of Prijedor was constituted. In September 1991, the Territorial Defence and the 5th Kozara Brigade were mobilised. This caused a great rift among the peoples because Serbs responded to the mobilisation while the Muslims largely avoided this obligation. When the SDA started calling on the Muslims not to go into the army, the rift became for more pronounced. A great influx of refugees occurred after the conflict in Croatia started. These were refugees of Serbian ethnicity. The influx primarily caused a great economic problem. In addition, it caused a great commotion among the inhabitants of Prijedor, owing to the events in World War II and the suffering of the Serbian people. As of the autumn of 1991, there was more and more talk about the illegal armament of the Muslims, while the Patriotic League and the Green Berets had already been mentioned earlier. Throughout the autumn, the SDS maintained contacts with the SDA and HDZ on both the political party level and in the organs in which they worked together. However, the increasing tension led to the foundation of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and of the Prijedor SDS Crisis Staff on 7th of January, 1992. The basic task of the Prijedor Crisis Staff was to follow the situation and events in and around Prijedor which were significant to the life of the citizens. On 17th of January, 1992, a decision was reached for Prijedor to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina since Banja Luka was the centre towards which Prijedor gravitated economically and politically. The municipalities never considered the ARK a creation whose documents should be binding for the municipal authorities. On 30th of April, Mr. Stakic learned from Simo Miskovic that Alija Delimustafic ordered the MUP to commence combat operations. Given the circumstances, it was decided that control ought to be taken of the town and that should be done by storm in order to avoid bloodshed. Everything was accomplished without a single bullet fired and none of the inhabitants was killed or even wounded. The basic goal of the authorities in Prijedor was to preserve peace and avoid an armed conflict. However, already in the beginning of May 1992, a Serbian policeman was killed. Nevertheless, the relatives of the killed policeman opted for revenge and killed four persons of Muslim ethnicity. This led to the introduction of a curfew and to a request to surrender illegal weapons. This appeal referred also to the citizens of Serbian ethnicity. The next attack happened in Hambarine on 22nd of May, 1992. Two days later, on 24th of May, an army column was again attacked on the Banja Luka-Prijedor road, from the direction of Kozarac. On 30th of May, 1992, members of Muslim forces carried out an organised, concentrated, and simultaneous attack against Prijedor, which was successfully repelled. During the fighting in Kozarac, a group of civilians turned up, moving in the direction of the town. The army let them through. Due to the large number of civilians in town, it was decided that they were -- they be directed towards Trnopolje. The population started moving out from Prijedor already in February and March 1992. The main reason for moving out were the constant clashes, the lack of electric power, water, and basic food provisions. Even after the main Muslim forces in the territory of Prijedor had been dispersed, there were many small and large groups remaining which constantly clashed with members of the VRS and the police. Nevertheless, Muslims and Croats lived in the territory of Prijedor throughout the entire war. It was never the plan of the municipal authorities of Prijedor to be a single-ethnicity municipality. Dr. Stakic met Dr. Karadzic several times during the war. He never heard him advocating the deportation of the Muslims and the Croats, or the creation of a mono-ethnic Serbian state. And that's the summary. And at that moment I do not have questions for Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stakic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing; that is, through your written statement. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. I take it you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, in your statement you acknowledge that you knew at the time of two major crimes committed by Bosnian Serb police and military forces against non-Serbs in Prijedor. The first is the massacre of dozens of Keraterm detainees by military, and that's at paragraph 24 of your statement; and the other one is another massacre of Muslims, this time by police officers, Muslims who were leaving Prijedor in a convoy at Koricanske Stijene, and that's at paragraph 30. And my question, Dr. Stakic, is: Aside from what you knew then, what you know now, as you sit here today, is that, in fact, the police and the army committed far more crimes against Muslims and Croats in Prijedor in 1992. They detained thousands of them in horrific conditions where they were subjected to torture and mistreatment, killed hundreds and hundreds of them, and destroyed their property on a massive scale. You know that now as you sit here today; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I just warn that "killed hundreds and hundreds" had been translated "thousands and thousands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If there's any difference, yes, it's "hundreds and hundreds." Yes, shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I gave a statement to the members of Mr. Karadzic's Defence team, I stated this on the basis of the knowledge that I had then, because these two things that happened were terrible. They are not less terrible than the others, but all the other citizens of Prijedor heard about that. It wasn't only me as president of the Municipal Assembly. You do know that I was at this trial, and during that trial and over all those years, although I'm in prison and I don't have much information from the ground, but during that trial I found out about many other crimes that did happen, unfortunately, in the municipality of Prijedor. And I agree with what is written in the trial judgement and the appeals judgement with regard to these crimes. And may I say straight away, that I personally or my defence during the trial before this court - my trial, that is - we never tried to deny or underestimate these crimes. Quite simply, we showed that that I was not a big player or the main player. I also agree with the statement made by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 616 in the trial judgement in my case. But again, may I say that I do not agree with those parts where it says that I'm the person in charge and that I'm responsible for all these crimes. I would like to take this opportunity to express my profound regret, which I did express during my own trial, for everything that was done to my fellow citizens in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stakic. That was a helpful but somewhat roundabout answer. I take it you agree with my summary of events in Prijedor in 1992, that the police and the army committed mass crime against Muslims and Croats in Prijedor, detentions, torture, mistreatment, and killings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think perhaps I was a bit lengthy in my answer, but I did say that these two crimes are horrible in themselves, but the other ones you mention are even more horrific, and they really happened. All I can do is express my regret, once again, that it happened. But as I was trying to say, at that time I did not know of all these crimes that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now at paragraph 16 of your statement, you describe the 30th of April, 1992, SDS take-over of Prijedor as a reaction to a fax from Mr. Delimustafic, dated the 29th of April, 1992. And at paragraph 33, you deny that the take-over was prepared well in advance of the 1st of May, 1992. And in fact, Dr. Stakic, the Prijedor SDS had been planning the take-over of Prijedor well before the 29th of April and that 29th of April telex was simply a trigger which accelerated the timing of the take-over; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I was not aware that the SDS was planning any take-over.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could look at D1830, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And as you can see, Dr. Stakic, these are the minutes of the SDS Municipal Board dated the 23rd of April, 1992. And if you look at point 5, towards the bottom of the page, it states a decision was taken "to immediately start working on the take-over, the co-ordination with the JNA, notwithstanding." Now that reflects that the SDS was planning to take-over the municipality well before receiving the 29th of April fax; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can look at that paragraph, but I should like to ask you to read the whole document. At the beginning there is a reference to who took part in the discussion, and the names are listed. And you don't see my name there. I can't say for sure whether I was at that session or not, because I didn't attend all the sessions. But from this, you can't see that I discussed anything. People were saying all sorts of things, and when I myself was looking for documents, I found another record, a longer one of that session, where Mr. Drljaca -- it's an extended document, P0041716 is the number. And 0041719. Simo Drljaca says: "We and Simo Miskovic were told today at the barracks that we would be arrested." And you see they are coming, and if somebody is threatening them there, I don't see how that can be called co-operation. Anyway, I'm just telling you my personal view. I had no impression and no knowledge that any take-over is being prepared. And on that day, 29 April, as I said in paragraph 16, I was in my office doing my usual job as vice president of the Municipal Assembly. I stayed there until 4.00 p.m. and then went home.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 05787, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Dr. Stakic, I see you have your statement in front of you and some other documents, and I will be referring to your statement so it's helpful that you have it. If you'd like to refer to any other documents besides your statement, if you could please inform us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now this is a 28th of April, 1994, "Kozarski Vjesnik" article, which includes an interview with you. We can see your photo there.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could look to the bottom, the last paragraph at the very bottom left-hand corner of the screen. If that could be blown up for you. So that paragraph at the -- in the bottom left-hand corner, it starts with you stating: "What happened on the 30th of April, 1992, was only the final act of a long-standing, but for the Serbs, perilous plan." Now, this is what you told "Kozarski Vjesnik" about the 30th of April take-over, that it was the final act of a long-standing plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read this. It says: "What happened on the 30th of April was just the finale of a plan long in the making fatal to the Serbs." So it means "fatal to the Serbs." I don't know how that was translated into English. Because it relates to the fax that we received, where they proclaimed the beginning of combat against Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this statement you made reflects, does it not, not only the advanced planning of the take-over but your knowledge of the fact that that take-over was planned in advance; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know how this statement of mine was translated into English. I would like the -- to ask the interpreters to interpret it. I said: "What happened on the 30th of April was just the finale of a plan long in the making that was fatal to the Serbs." "A plan," meaning prepared by the HDZ and the SDA and that they revealed in the fax sent by the minister of the interior. I didn't say here that Serbs had been preparing anything for a long time. And I say further that they had been arming themselves secretly, sewing uniforms, et cetera. And later on I got hold of some information seized by the army and the police, documents from which we saw that they had indeed been preparing a long time for that, and later on in the newspapers they tried to deny that fax.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S and stay on the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention to the very top left-hand corner in the B/C/S. And here you refer to the Muslims secretly arming themselves, making uniforms with the symbol of the lily, building strongholds in Kozara. Then you say: "But we were not just sitting there idle. When we saw what they were doing, we began to arm ourselves and to tell the party members what they were planning to do to us and what has to be done to prevent 1941 happening all over again." Now in your statement you emphasize the arming and organising activities of the Muslim side, but you don't say anything about such activities on the Serb side. But in this article, you acknowledged that the Serbs were indeed arming themselves with your knowledge and support; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago I was able to see the date of this statement I made to the press. What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the 28th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I said a moment ago as well that when I was giving this statement, I was trying to describe the knowledge that I had then in that period, from January until October 1992. And this is 1994. During the war, our officers spoke to the radio, to the newspapers, and our police did too. And from the things they said, I learnt that they had also been working to arm Serbian people. But that's something I learned later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Gustafson, do you agree that English translation that we have is not correct? First page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I understood it to be slightly different, but I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not "Serb plan," it's "perilous plan to Serbs" --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yeah, "for the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We will request a revision of this translation. And if we could move to page 2 of the English and move down the page, about two-thirds of the way down the page in the B/C/S, still on the far left-hand side. And this is about a third of the way down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You state here: "We knew they were armed mainly with zoljas, infantry weapons, and wasps, but we had better military potential and our lads were brave and bold." Now, here you acknowledged that the Serb side was better armed than the Muslim side. And that's true as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat once again: This is something I learned later. The commander of the brigade which participated in the fighting gave an interview describing which units took part, with what weapons and equipment. So in 1994, I already knew about these things. But in March, April, May 1992, I did not have that information because nobody owed it to me to inform me, nor was I superior to the army or the police for them to report to me about the equipment and assets they dispose of.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go back to page 1 of the English and back up to the top of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is about six lines down in the B/C/S and two-thirds of the way down in the English. You state: "On the direction of the central office of the SDS, we formed the Serbian Assembly of Prijedor on 7th January 1992, and I became chairman." Now, this is a reflection of the fact that you established the Serbian Assembly in Prijedor pursuant to republic level SDS instructions; in particular, the Variant A and B instructions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in my statement. The SDS president convened the session. I believe that was before this 7th of January. I believe it was in December. And at that session, he showed us that document. The document was not copied and distributed to everybody. He just showed it to us and read it out, saying that there are Variants A and B. One of them does not apply to us because we did not have the majority in the Assembly. The other one applies to us, and we should follow that other variant and organise the Serbian Assembly in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the first two pages of this would be admitted, but there is another article and the rest of it that probably shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, that makes sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit this part of the article. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6581, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Stakic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, by the way --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- I take it the parties were informed of the extended sitting schedule that was planned. Okay. It was just sent. But you will stick to the three hours allocated to you, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I -- I certainly intend to. It's always difficult to predict these things with certainty, but I would note that even with the three hours, it doesn't seem -- seems like it may be very difficult to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do your best to conclude your cross in three hours. And I -- for the Defence, it will have less than 40 or 50 minutes for the redirect, if we are to conclude Mr. Stakic's evidence today at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Between 40 and 50 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My calculation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That should be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will sit until 4.00 today. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, at paragraph 18 you describe an attack on a military vehicle carrying five VRS members in Hambarine on the 22nd of May, 1992. And you describe a similar attack on Kozarac -- attacking Kozarac on the 24th of May. And you state: "These attacks were responded to." Now, with respect to events in Hambarine, the Crisis Staff -- Prijedor Crisis Staff issued an ultimatum to hand over the alleged perpetrators of this incident, and stated that if this ultimatum was not complied with, the Crisis Staff was no longer willing to guarantee the safety of the population -- the civilian population of the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you and what's written in paragraph 18, with all due respect. As for that other part, I don't know. To the best of my knowledge, the Crisis Staff met for the first time on the 29th of May. So it couldn't possibly issue this, nor was it within the purview of the Crisis Staff. But maybe you have some other document saying the contrary. But the fact is the Crisis Staff was established on the 29th of May at a regular Assembly session, and I don't remember that it was convened specially because of these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to P3485, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention to the article at the top right-hand side of this page in the B/C/S. And this is a 29th of May, 1992, "Kozarski Vjesnik" -- page from "Kozarski Vjesnik" which recites public statements of the Crisis Staff. And this one on the top right is a statement dated the 23rd of May, 1992. And the column -- in the column on the far right-hand side - and in the English this is the last two paragraphs on the first page - it states that: "The Crisis Staff hereby orders the population of Hambarine local commune and other local communes in the area ... to hand over the perpetrators of this crime ... by Saturday, the 23rd of May." And the final paragraph states: "This crime has exhausted all dead-lines and promises and the Crisis Staff no longer can, nor is it willing to, guarantee the security of the population of the above-mentioned villages in this area."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see now this article and it's signed "Crisis Staff." You know, in the Crisis Staff we also had a press officer or something to that effect who had the right -- not only had the right, but it was his job to meet with the media and issue press releases. Sometimes he would sign these releases "press officers," sometimes he would sign them "Crisis Staff." But if you ever saw a decision of the Crisis Staff itself, it's usually signed "president of the Crisis Staff" and my name underneath, because I was the president. So this press release was made by the press officer, because the army had also spoken to the radio on the same day, and he made a statement on behalf of the Crisis Staff. Also, a moment ago mobilisation was mentioned. The mobilisation call-ups are signed by the minister of defence, and we at the municipal level don't have the power to cancel it or prohibit it, but what we could do is address the press and appeal on the radio to all able-bodied men over 18 to respond to the call-up. So this is not a decision or the opinion of the Crisis Staff. It's the opinion of the press officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, when the perpetrators were not handed over by the population of Hambarine, the army attacked the village, shelling the village, attacking the population as a whole, and destroying the homes -- destroying homes of the Muslims who lived there; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned and heard that these things happened during those days, but I cannot tell you anything more about the extent and the substance of that operation because they had no obligation to keep me informed about what was really going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 19 of your statement, you discuss the 30th of May attack against Prijedor town by Muslim forces, an attack which you explained was repelled within a matter of hours. What you don't state anywhere in your statement is that after this attack was repelled, the army virtually destroyed the largely Muslim neighbourhood of Stari Grad in Prijedor town; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? As I described it here, that night I was in the building of the Municipal Assembly when the attack started. I heard the shooting. And at first, I thought it was soldiers shooting in the air, as they usually do when they are going to the front line or coming back. But then stronger explosions started, like grenades and even stronger, around the Assembly building itself. Then I went into the hallway, and the shooting was coming from the park, which was only 150 metres away from the building. The few of us civilians who were in the building at that time were not armed, but fortunately, outside the municipality building there was a check-point manned by two or three soldiers or policemen, I am not sure, who were armed. And I don't know if you know what it looks like. Next to the municipal building, there is the police station, and they also had reserve policemen there who were armed. And shooting was heard from that side as well. It lasted until about 9.00, when I saw a tank, a Serbian tank between the SUP building and our building, and I saw troops coming in, and then they moved towards the park, the new buildings, and the -- the buildings and the new hotel where the explosions were coming from. And they started moving towards Stari Grad, the old town. I wasn't there in the old town but I heard that it was considerably devastated. I don't know if the army really had to respond that way and use that kind of force. It's not up to me to judge. I'm not a soldier. I'm not qualified. But at any rate, it was not my purpose to devastate and destroy the town. There were socially owned buildings there, public buildings, and there were Serb businesses and facilities that were damaged or destroyed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said that you "don't know if the army really had to respond that way and use that kind of force. It's not up to me to judge. I'm not a soldier." But in fact, you called a military expert in your case, a US general, General Wilmot, and I'd like to remind you of what he said in response to questions from your lawyer in your trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this has been uploaded at 65 ter 25618.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He was asked the question: "Help me with this: Also the military at this point, did they continue to pursue or were they in pursuit of the 'enemy' as a result of the May 30th, 1992, attack upon the city/town of Prijedor?" And he answered: "Yes, they did pursue the attacking forces, but they also stopped in I guess I would describe it as a suburb neighbourhood. I've never been there so I don't know exactly how to describe it. Called Stari Grad, is it? And they decimated that neighbourhood which is contrary to the rules of land warfare and probably criminal action if one would take a look at it, and if certain -- and if authorities would examine what happened there, it was an atrocity, and something that the army should have been brought to account on." Now, that was what your defence military expert said about what the army did in Stari Grad after they repelled this attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly what he said, with all due respect. I trust what you've said, that you're reading it out as he said it. As you said yourself, he's a military expert. He can say that. However, I cannot. I was not at the old town. I heard that it was destroyed in that operation. And I said a moment ago I don't know whether there was that use of force, this excessive use of force, as this expert said, or whether it was proportionate. I really wouldn't want to go into all of that. You see, once again, I'm saying: I'm 50 years old now. At that time, I was only 29 years old. I was just a new, inexperienced doctor, politically unqualified, naive, not to speak of the military and the police. These were not departments that were within my line of work. I was not in charge of them on the basis of any documents, and especially in view of my age and lack of experience, I could not have any kind of supervision over the army or could I exert any kind of pressure over them. I just tried here, this paragraph -- I just happened to be there, so I'm speaking as a witness, and I saw what was happening around me. Because later on I did find out, but I really didn't want to go into all of that. Also, on the under -- on the other side, where the underpass is, there were wounded people. And then the commander of the military got killed near Kozarski Vjesnik, and also many policemen were killed at the bridge. Later on I found out that the attackers had come over the Sana because the bridge was guarded by the military and the police, and they came from the direction of the old town. And apparently, they were withdrawing at that point. But I'm telling you all of this as a citizen who heard later about what was going on. I don't want underestimate the report of that expert. Namely, that what happened there did happen. I'm not trying to diminish it. I'm not trying to deny it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Gustafson, can you scroll back to lines 1 of this page, page 36. It's part of your reading from that expert's testimony, "called Stari Grad, is it," and the afterwards, probably because you read too fast, something is missing, before you referred to criminal action. I heard -- I remember something to the effect of that's contrary to warfare or something? Could you read it again slowly?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. "And they decimated that neighbourhood, which is contrary to the rules of land warfare and probably criminal action ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Stakic, at paragraph 51 of your statement you comment on adjudicated fact 1267, relating to the destruction of non-Serb settlements, and you said that, as far as you were aware, it was not just Muslim homes that were destroyed. And you gave the example of Mr. Srdjo Srdic [phoen], a Serb, and you state that his house which was in the immediate vicinity of the municipal building was damaged during the combat activities. Now, Mr. Srdic provided evidence about the destruction -- or the damage to his home that the Defence has submitted, and this is what he said about it. "Mine was the only Serb house in Prijedor that was burnt down. They wanted to kill me. They wanted to liquidate me. And the proof of that is that they threw an explosive device on my balcony, and prior to that they put 'SDA' on it. But this was not done by a Muslim."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that's at D2265, page 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now it's clear from Mr. Srdic's evidence that his house wasn't damaged in the course of combat. He was singled out among Serbs in Prijedor and his home was specifically targeted for personal reasons; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that statement of Mr. Srdic's. I remember that he used to come to the Municipal Assembly. You know, down there at the executive board, there is this department for property-related matters. First of all, he wanted to prove that it was his house -- actually, he lived in another house. And this is a shop. It's right in front of the Municipal Assembly building. It's not even 50 metres away. I mean, I was not watching all the time because I sought shelter behind a wall. I wasn't looking through the window. I didn't want to be hit myself. I don't know whether it was hit by a Muslim tank or a Serb zolja. I'm not going into all of that. But during that fighting, the shop was damaged because these are houses that share walls. These are not stand-alone houses. They're attached. You can see that if you go out into the ground. It's 50 metres from the entrance into the Municipal Assembly. And here my answer pertains to that. I mean, I'm not denying that -- well, Stari Grad, the old town, as far as I know, had a majority Muslim population, and these houses were destroyed. I, as a human being, can just express my regret for the fact that these buildings were destroyed, as I did then. But Mr. Srdic came to speak to us and he said that he would be seeking damages. Also, these people from Kozarac, a delegation came to see me, and they came to report the damage that had been sustained by their houses. Now, what he personally thinks, I really wouldn't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, now you're -- I'd like to ask you now about Trnopolje, the facility you speak about in your statement. As I understand it, your evidence is that during and after the attack on Kozarac, the civilians fled the area, the army allowed them to pass. They arrived in Prijedor town and then someone directed them to Trnopolje, which you refer to as a holding centre. And that's paragraphs 18 and 22. And so now as I understand it, your position is that this movement of civilians out of Kozarac and to Trnopolje was a movement that happened on their own, they moved on their own, and they moved voluntarily to Trnopolje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I read this once again and see what is written here? With all due respect, I don't see that I say at any point that these people voluntarily, and so on and so forth, madam. I'm saying here this information that I received. I set out in the morning, I left my parents house, and they live in the village of Mariska, and that is where I had moved my wife and my young child. Why? Because there was no electricity. My parents didn't have any electricity either but they live in the country, so they have a well. They also have a stove that is fired by wood. I'm sorry for saying all of this right now. And at the check-point the police said: No, you cannot pass this way because there is fighting underway. And then I took the roundabout way by Rakelici and Cela. I arrived in Prijedor. By the time I got to work it was - I don't know - about midday. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but my time is very limited and I think you're more or less repeating what's in your statement. Let me try to ask it in a clearer way. I think my question could have been clearer. I take it your position is that the Muslims of Kozarac went -- ended up in Trnopolje and they went there on their own. Nobody captured them and put them there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam, I do apologise, but that is not written in my statement, that they did this voluntarily. I'm trying to explain to you how it was that I found out about this. Because in some statement out there, I mean, in some report that appeared later by the MUP, they claim that the Crisis Staff founded Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm, you know, and they are not referring to any date or the number of that decision or whatever. I'll telling you how it was that I learned about this. I'm not saying it was voluntary at all. There were operations going on there. It's the army then, that there, at the front line, opened a passageway, if that's the right word, and then they let these people get to town, because they had set out towards town from Kozarac. And then, the people I worked with at the Assembly told me that they had arrived during the night and that they were staying in two buildings in town. And most of them were called upon to stay with their relatives, friends. There were people with mixed marriages and so on and so forth. I don't know who took these people in. At one point in time, when the police realised that these buildings were overcrowded, they took buses. Once again, they asked these people whether anybody had some private apartment or house to stay at with someone, and then they got these other people who had fled from Kozarac from the fighting, and then they channeled them towards Trnopolje. I never said - and I don't want to say it now, too, and I don't want this to be put to me - that they went voluntarily. What happened to them is really sad and I regret it. But I'm not saying we did not make any decision about this Trnopolje. We did not plan this Trnopolje. At least, I did not take part in that and I'm not aware of any such thing. I'm not saying then and I'm not saying now that they voluntarily left their homes in order to go somewhere, even if you call it a holding centre or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Your position on that is now clear. Thank you. Now you said that you never said they went voluntarily, "what happened to them is really sad, and I regret it. But I'm not saying we did not make any decision about this, Trnopolje. We did not plan this Trnopolje." And what the Crisis Staff did do, Dr. Stakic, is control the manner in which people could be released from Trnopolje, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff to control this? This Trnopolje was not under the Crisis Staff. And as far as I know, Mr. Kuruzovic, Slobodan Kuruzovic, was appointed on behalf of the army, and those who appointed him were supposed to receive reports from him in terms of what was going on in the centre. It's not that I was supposed to receive reports or the Crisis Staff. It is a fact that people, but mainly from the Red Cross, the local Red Cross that was down there, they did address the Crisis Staff. But they were asking for assistance in terms of food, medicine, medical supplies, and later on oil because they also organised the transportation for these unfortunate people.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P2915, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, you can see that about two-thirds of the way down the page there it says: A summary of conclusions, orders, and decisions adopted by the Crisis Staff from the 29th of May to the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And near the top in the B/C/S, in your -- towards the bottom in the English, one of the conclusions it refers to is conclusion number 01-1-023-45/92 of the 2nd of July, 1992, forbidding the individual release of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm. A moment ago you referred to the Red Cross coming to the Crisis Staff asking for assistance in terms of food, medicine, and oil. This decision summarised here reflects the Crisis Staff's control over the manner in which people are released from this facility where you acknowledge people were held in a very sad state. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this question of yours, there are several assertions, several sub-questions, if you will, but I will try to answer as clear as possible. First of all, to the best of my knowledge, then and now, as far as Omarska and Keraterm are concerned, it was the police that was in charge. As for Trnopolje, it was the army who was in charge. How come, I do not know. I cannot explain. Secondly, the Crisis Staff is a collective body. There were 11 of us there. I explained to you a moment ago when I said that I was not present every time, because we would work one day and then I'd go home and then I'd come again, and if you look at the decisions of the Crisis Staff, you will see that only about 30 per cent were signed by me. So even if I was absent, it was enough to have six members there to pass a decision, out of the total of 11. This word "conclusion," that's not an order. We could not issue orders to the army or to the police in terms of what they would do there. Now, this is some kind of opinion on my part. Sometimes, people on the basis of certain interventions -- well, I know of Dr. Beglerbegovic, I didn't even know that he had been arrested and it just says that he released from Omarska because the people got together and signed a petition for him to be released. And then I know about a former football player from Partizan, they called the chief of SUP and then he was released too. And so on. To the best of my knowledge, it was the local Red Cross that operated there and then later on the International Red Cross became involved too. And they turned to us for this kind of logistical support as I said a moment ago. I don't know what else I could really tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Stakic, you are insisting - and you've done that several times, that you -- these facilities were not operated by the Crisis Staff, Trnopolje was operated by the army, and that you couldn't issue orders to them. But this conclusion reflects the understanding of the Crisis Staff members at the time, that they had the power to forbid the individual release of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout all that time, and again I'm telling you that I could not issue any orders to Mr. Drljaca to release somebody or to keep him there. I claim that with full responsibility. I could have written an order a day, but none of those orders would have been binding on anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do Your Honours wish to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Given the circumstances, the Chamber is minded to reduce the lunch break to 40 minutes. We resume at 10 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And if I could have P2741, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, this is a 2nd of June, 1992, Prijedor Crisis Staff decision on the release of imprisoned persons. It orders the release of various categories of persons, such as Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake, under Article 1; Article 4, all persons older than 60 for whom an investigation has confirmed that they did not commit an offence, and a few other categories. And in the last article which is on the next page in the English it says that the public security station is in charge implementing this decision, and the chief of SJB is personally responsible for it. Now this -- if we go to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, this document is signed by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, just before the break you said: "I'm telling you that I could not issue any orders to Drljaca to release somebody or keep him there." That was at page 44. But this document demonstrates you doing exactly that, you're ordering Drljaca to release certain categories of prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you will allow me, this is what I wanted to say when answering your previous question. Unfortunately, I was not the one who established the Crisis Staff or the decided on its composition. However, what I realised during my trial in 2002, the secretary of the Municipal Assembly was not a member of that Crisis Staff. He was a lawyer. When I saw that ten years later during my trial and now 20 years later, I can see that some of the things were established without any foundation in the prevalent law and that's how things were drafted. Mr. Drljaca was a lawyer and he worked for the police. I didn't even know that there were detained Serbs there. It was only when we received that information from him that I learned it, that some of them were army and police members as is written here, and they had not responded to the mobilisation call. And in keeping with that, our position was that they should not be there. We wanted to avoid any problems in that centre. And it's a fact. However, this is a decision, not an order. He could implement it or not. As I have already told you, we had other examples of people who were moving out after having moved into an apartment illegally. That's when we sought assistance of the police. But it was not an order. It was just a request on our part to seek the help of the police when it came to moving those people out. And when you asked me just a while ago about certain individuals, it did happen, you know, that individuals would go to those centres and they would take people away for their own personal gain in order to extort money from them --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and even sadder than that --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, I'm really not asking you about the reasons why you issued this decision. Just the fact that it was issued, and if you could really try to focus on my specific questions because of my time limitations. Now, you said in your answer: "It was just a request on our part to seek the help of the police." Now, this decision, as you can see in Article 6, states that the public security station "shall be in charge of the implementation of this decision and the chief of the public security station shall be deemed personally responsible for it ..." This is not phrased as a request, is it? This is phrased in mandatory terms; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, Madam, as you know. But when I look at the title, it says "a decision," not "an order." And as far as I knew then and now, Simo Drljaca was the person who was responsible. He behaved the way he did, he reported to his superiors as to what he was doing. He did not have to inform us. There are other decisions of ours and our requests to which he responded. Most often he would tell us: Do your job. Don't interfere with mine, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P2637, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, as you can see, this is a 1st of July, 1992, SJB document sent to the Crisis Staff. And the reference -- it refers to two, what it says "your documents," presumably Crisis Staff documents. And it states: "In reference to your documents of the above numbers and dates, we hereby inform you that ..." And the first entry states that: "Conclusion number 02-111-108/92, by which the release of prisoners is prohibited is being fully observed." Now this reflects, does it not, Mr. Drljaca's implementation of a Crisis Staff decision prohibiting the release of prisoners and his report back to the Crisis Staff to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to repeat once again -- or, rather, you didn't allow me to finish a minute ago. When it comes to those individuals, what we meant was that those people, Serbs, if I may call them criminals, they would go to those centres, they would take away individuals from there for their own personal gain. They would extort cars from them and money. And the saddest thing of all is that they would not return them. They would kill them. That was our objection. It was not that we were interfering with their work, that they were not allowed to release prisoners. And then if you'll allow me, look at the last conclusion with regard to the establishment of the infamous intervention platoon. Together with the military police they --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you immediately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat. Together with the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, if we could go to the next page in the English, to the top of the page. I think that's what Dr. Stakic is referring to now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, I'm not sure what you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I am not sure what paper you have now in front of you, but if I could ask you to focus on the document that's on the screen and answer the question -- answer the questions relating to that document.
