utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the same document, madam. In the Serbian version the paragraph is at the bottom of the page, and it's about the order dated 17 June, whereby Mr. Drljaca answers that an integrated intervention platoon was established. And I claim with full responsibility that I never learnt about its establishment. I was never informed about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Stakic, this document is directed to the Crisis Staff, and it states clearly that that intervention platoon was formed and gives information on what it has been doing. Are you saying that you never received this document that was addressed to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that I did not receive the document. I am saying -- and I have something that you probably have as well. This is an order by the Crisis Staff on the establishment of that intervention platoon. The number is D2039. And another P0048598. This is the original decision of the Crisis Staff. I don't know whether you are able to broadcast the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that document at the moment, Dr. Stakic. Let me ask you this: In your statement at paragraph 21, you said that the Crisis Staff could not give orders either to the army or the police. And at paragraph 24, you said that Drljaca's most frequent answer to you and others in the Crisis Staff was to leave him alone to do his job and that you do yours. And you've repeated that sentiment today. This document paints a very different picture. It reflects the SJB reporting directly to the Crisis Staff on the implementation of a number of Crisis Staff decisions, such as the release of prisoners, the intervention platoons, closing catering establishments, prohibitions on shooting. This document is -- contradicts your position on the Crisis Staff authority over the police, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, I don't agree with that assertion. And I am trying to ask you to read this document to see what was asked from Mr. Drljaca, and then you look at his answer and you will see that his answer is completely different. Answers to a different question -- or, rather, his answer is not truthful. This is what I'm saying. As MPs in the Assembly and the Crisis Staff was just a -- the continuation of the Assembly. It was a small-scale Assembly, if I may put it that way, and the chief of the public security station once a year submitted a report to the Assembly about the security situation in the municipality. Since the Assembly MPs asked me to ask Simo Drljaca to write that report, he did it. But what I'm saying is that what he wrote was one thing and his actions were different. It was requested from him to establish a platoon composed of 20 members of the police and 20 members of the army. Look at his report. He did not establish a mixed platoon. He claims that he has an intervention platoon which co-operates with the army. And it's an entirely different thing. And this is what I'm trying to say to you. Once again, as far as I know, in Bosanska Krupa and in Samac, the military and the police arrested the president of the municipality and president of the Executive Board, and I have no information to the contrary; i.e., that the president of the municipality arrested the chief of the police or the commander of the -- of a unit. It was absolutely impossible according to our legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, this report from Drljaca about prohibition of releasing prisoners is related to the conclusion we saw earlier on today?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, I think it's a different conclusion related --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Date is --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- to the same subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Date is different and the number is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mm-hm. No, I was just addressing the witness's claim that he couldn't issue any orders to Drljaca either to release or detain prisoners, and both of these documents contradict that. But they don't relate to the same decision. No, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, I'd like to go back to what you said in relation to the Crisis Staff conclusion prohibiting the release of prisoners that's reflected in this police document, and you said: "When it comes to those individuals, what we meant was that these people, Serbs, if I may call them criminals, they would go to those centres, they would take away individuals from there for their own personal gain. They would extort them -- or cars from them or money, and the saddest thing of all was that they would not return them. They would kill them. That was our objection. It was not that we were interfering with their work, that they were not allowed to release prisoners." That was at page 48. So I take it that the Crisis Staff -- that you in the Crisis Staff were aware at the time that people were going to centres like Omarska, taking out prisoners, and killing them, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information to that effect. And that was our attempt to appeal to those people there to do their job. If those people -- those wretched people were detained and if they were being interrogated as they claimed, they shouldn't allow such things to happen. I'm sure that you have a document because I've seen it during my trial. I had a report from Simo Drljaca - not me, but the Assembly - in which he claimed that only two individuals were killed in Omarska; i.e., not killed but died of natural causes, you know. And he signed that report. It was an official report. I wasn't there. I couldn't go there. I -- I did not have the means to carry out my own investigation. What could I do at the moment or what can I do now? I can just express my regret for not having resigned. Eventually I did. I did resign and my resignation was adopted in January 1993. That was one of the ways I expressed my dissatisfaction. Maybe I should have done it earlier when I first realised that there was nothing I could do to prevent all those things from happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So at paragraph 24 of your witness statement, when you -- where you say that "at the time I knew about two natural deaths that occurred at the Omarska centre but that is the only thing I know with regard to Omarska," that's not really true, is it, because you're saying now that you knew that people were -- Serbs were taking prisoners away and killing them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat word for word what I have just stated. This is what I received. I provided my statement based on what I received from Mr. Drljaca as an official report about how many people died there, but we knew that from Keraterm and Trnopolje - and Trnopolje was the least protected of all - people would be taken away by armed individuals. I don't know how many people were taken away. I don't know who did it. But it did happen and this was our attempt to appeal to the police and to the security over there not to allow those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 20 of your statement, you refer to the decision on the organisation and work of Crisis Staff, which is P3536. And Article 2 of that decision says that the Crisis Staff's responsibilities included co-ordinating the protection of safety of people and property. Now that accurately reflects the Crisis Staff's responsibilities towards the safety and security of citizens of Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have that document from which you quoted? Can I see it? I don't have any doubts that the way you quoted was correct, but I'd like to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we can go to P3536, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the article that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's Article 2, which refers to the Crisis Staff's responsibility for, among other things, co-ordinating the protection of safety of people and property. You agree that that was among the Crisis Staff's responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, madam? The Crisis Staff or the presidency -- and the term "presidency" was reinstated. I don't know why the term "Crisis Staff" was introduced in the first place or at least I don't understand that. These are the remains of the communist system. At that time, we couldn't change the documents based on which such bodies were established. And within that system, the entire population was military. We were all soldiers. We were all duty-bound to participate in the country's defence. We -- and this is why things were drafted the way they were. Without any clear instructions to the effect that the Crisis Staff was subordinate to the police or the army. The term used here is "co-ordination," but according to what I know, the Crisis Staff was not subordinate -- superior to the police forces and certainly not the military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At the beginning of your testimony, you stated at page 24: "I also agree with the statement made by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 616 of the trial judgement. And that paragraph states that: "The Trial Chamber does not believe that the conscious object of Dr. Stakic's participation in the creation and maintenance of this environment of impunity was to kill the non-Serb citizens of Prijedor municipality. However, it is satisfied that Dr. Stakic, in his various positions, acted in the knowledge that the existence of such an environment would in all likelihood result in killings, and that he reconciled himself to and made peace with this probable outcome. He consequently participated with the requisite dolus eventualis and therefore incurs criminal responsibility for all the killings in paragraphs 44 and 47 of the indictment, which the Trial Chamber has found to be proven." So I take it from your agreement with this paragraph that you were aware at the time that the environment in Prijedor was extremely -- an extremely dangerous one for the non-Serb population, an environment which would in all likelihood result in killings of members of this population; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know if it's in the trial transcript, but I said I agree with the initial sentence, the first sentence. However, where the Trial Chamber found that I was not aware that all non-Serbs were being killed, I agree about that part. But I don't agree, as I said before, with those passages in the judgement that say that I was a major player and decision maker. As for the knowledge I gained over the past 20 years in France and the US, where I served my sentence, in those places a mayor can appoint the local chief of police. That's very different from our equivalent of mayor who had no competence over the army or the police. And I also want to add, when I was 29 and had just graduated from medical school, I was politically illiterate and I certainly had no personal authority to achieve something like that; whereas the regulations and the laws certainly didn't allow me to do that. As for the killings, unfortunately I learned about them later when they had already happened. And I can only say, once again, that I am sincerely sorry for everything that had happened to my fellow citizens in that period. And now looking back and thinking what could I have done, the only answer I come up with is that I could have resigned. I could have done that in July or August when I first found out about these events, but I don't want to deny --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but your answer is moving away from the question. My time is very limited and I would like to ask you to please focus on my questions. Earlier today you said: "We did not plan this Trnopolje. Trnopolje, at least I did not take part in that and I'm not aware of any such thing." That's page 41. And at paragraph 23 of your statement you said: "As far as investigation centres Keraterm and Omarska are concerned, the Crisis Staff did not participate in the formation of these centres." But in fact, all three of these centres were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that in the report by Mr. Drljaca where he claimed that those centres had been established based on decisions of the Crisis Staff. However, he never says which decisions, which date, which numbers, where he -- whereas he had legal training. He could have given references. Therefore, I stand by my earlier response, that I believe the Crisis Staff did not establish these centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 40126, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, Ms. Gustafson and Mr. Robinson, the document we saw in the -- by the number Exhibit P2915, which is the summary of conclusions taken by the Crisis Staff in the year of 1992, I note that it was admitted only for the -- some limited purpose. It was admitted for the -- only as a source document of Ms. Hanson. I think we can now admit it in full. Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6582, Your Honours -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it will be received, 2915, but it was fully admitted, not only as a source document. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, this is a transcript of a video-recorded interview with you. And it states -- you state near the beginning that you've been president of the Municipal Assembly for six or seven months, which would put the timing of this interview sometime around late 1992. Now, do you recall giving a video-recorded interview to an English-speaking reporter who had a translator with him around this time, late 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was more than one foreign reporter who came. I don't remember all of them. I'm looking at this document now. It's very possible, especially if it was recorded, that it was my interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I could direct your attention, Dr. Stakic, to about two-thirds of the way down the page in your language. This is about halfway down in English, where you're speaking and you state: "These places, such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, were a necessity in a given moment and were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor." And the reporter asks you: "So those three camps, or how are they ...?" And then you interrupt and say: "Reception centres." The reporter says: "... reception centres were formed according to the decision of your civilian authorities?" And you answer: "Yes, yes." Now, a moment ago when I put to you that you these centres were established by the civilian authorities, you said you read that in Drljaca's report. And in fact, this is what you stated at the time to the reporter; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned Drljaca's report a moment ago, he claimed that it was the Crisis Staff that established them, not the civilian authorities. As for this interview, I said there were military authorities and civilian authorities. The army had its own military police, military courts, military remand prisons; whereas the civilian authorities, apart from the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Board, they had the municipal court, the civilian police. All these were bodies of civilian authorities, at least as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, when I asked you the question I said: "These centres were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor; right?" And you didn't say, "Yes, yes," like you said in this interview. You said, "I read that in a report by Mr. Drljaca," and you went on to deny the accuracy of that report; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just said, no, I did not answer that way. I don't know how it was interpreted to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do you agree that those reception centres were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am trying to tell you what I understood, what I understand by "civilian authorities," because there is a division where we live into military authorities and civilian authorities. And I'm repeating: The military has its troops for military intervention, military police, military courts, et cetera; whereas the civilian authorities are the Municipal Assembly, the Executive Board, the municipal court, the civilian prosecutor's office, the civilian public defender, and the civilian police. And it is the civilian police that opened these centres because the civilian police is a part of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 5 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, if I could direct your attention to a passage approximately two-thirds of the way down the page, and roughly the same place in the English, in fact. And this again is you speaking. You're giving quite a long statement here. And about in the middle of it you say: "Those of us who have lived here for centuries, I mean the Serbs and the other peoples, I also mean the Muslims, who were created artificially, who were against the Serbs in the previous two wars, while the Serbs were on the side of the allies both times." Now, this statement of yours that the Muslims were artificially created, that's an offensive and discriminatory remark towards Muslims, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a faultless man. I never said I was. I am not without blame, and I'm not looking to wash myself of all that I've done here. But you must take into account that this was wartime. There was propaganda on both sides, and I probably stated something like this being carried away. What I meant was that from the Ottoman Empire's time, in our territory, the Muslims used to be Serbs who converted during Ottoman times to the Muslim faith. I am sorry now for anyone whom I offended with this statement, and nowadays I certainly would not allow myself to say something ugly like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you said it was ugly. You agree it's discriminatory and offensive; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you put it like that, it could be offensive. But please look at some other passages in this text where I said that our objective is to work for peace and --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- after the establishing of peace, we will continue to live together.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I am not asking you about other passages. I'm asking you about this passage. You agree that this is offensive and discriminatory towards Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I really don't know anymore what you want from me. I told you it was a mistake that I said this, and I'm really sorry about it and I agree with you that it sounds offensive. But please, just in order not to take it all out of context, you could quote some other things that I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to page 7 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is right at the top of the page in the B/C/S and the middle of the page in the English. You're being asked about the Muslims who used to live in Kozarac. And you say: "Well, Trnopolje was mainly filled with Muslims from Kozarac. A good part of those extremists were from Kozarac and they went to Trnopolje. The 1500 and some men who were moved with the help of the International Red Cross to Karlovac were mostly from Kozarac." And then a few lines down you say: "The rest, because their family homes had been destroyed, were accommodated either in the territory of Prijedor municipality or went, were transferred to ... some did go to Central Bosnia ... those who expressed this wish. We organised buses and a train for them, and this was for free, just that they go, so that there should be no casualties, that that genocide that we have already been blamed for in Europe should not occur." Now, when you said you organised buses and trains for Muslims from Trnopolje to transport them to Central Bosnia, are you referring to the municipal authorities? When you say "we organised buses and trains," is that something the municipal authorities did?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. That's not what I meant then and I don't mean it now. I meant the Red Cross that was there and organised it, and we just provided assistance at their request in transport and fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you provided the buses, the trains, and the fuel, the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You must understand one thing: Under the Law On All People's Defence, the army and the police are entitled to commandeer all means of transport, all the vehicles from all businesses, including bus companies and railway companies. They have the right to commandeer vehicles or trains or take over one entire enterprise, one entire company under that law. I'm telling you, it's not us who organised that. I'm telling you that the Red Cross approached us to provide fuel. They usually approached the Executive Board or perhaps the Crisis Staff, and we tried to accommodate them because they had already agreed with the ICRC, that's the way they explained it, they had agreed all the routes, et cetera, and we just had to provide assistance in that one aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, have we assigned an exhibit number for this witness's Rule 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It was done as part of the associated exhibits package that was given to us, and it's D4195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, you said you did this, you organised the transport so that there should be no casualties and in order to avoid a genocide. You are acknowledging here that the non-Serb population risked their lives by staying in Prijedor, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned genocide and you didn't finish the sentence: "... genocide for which we have already been blamed in Europe." I'm telling you again I have information now, from reading materials during my own trial, showing that certain groups of these extremists had been captured around Kozara in the hills of Kurevo in 1994 and even 1995. But Serbs, either soldiers or policemen, raided those areas, and on their own initiative, in addition to the regular police and army operations, they searched the houses of those people, looted, took their property --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and we had no means of protecting --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but you're not answering my question. You're talking about events in 1994 and 1995. This interview was around late 1992, and you're talking about the Muslims from Kozarac. And you said: "We organised buses and trains for them, just so that they go, so that there should be no casualties, that that genocide that we have already been blamed for in Europe should not occur." Now, those are your words, and by those words you are acknowledging that the non-Serbs who stayed in Prijedor did so at risk of their lives; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat once again, it's not us who organised it. It's the Red Cross. I agree with you insofar as you say that in that period it was very risky to live in Prijedor, for all the citizens, and it was especially risky for Muslims. I must add that it is regrettable they had to leave. But from a humane point of view, I still believe that they were better off, those who left and had a chance to return, than those who were killed. I'm not saying it was a good thing they had to go. It was a humiliation. But as our people say, as long as you live, you have a chance to start anew and rebuild your life.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 8 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is right near the top of the page in your language. It's near the middle of the page in the English. And you're being asked to respond to Western press allegations about ethnic cleansing. And in the course of your answer, you said: "I have already said at the beginning that most of them are leaving now partly for political reasons, but more for economic reasons. Because we are currently all endangered here. I once had a salary equivalent to 1.000 German marks. Now, as the mayor, I have 60 marks, and I am a subtenant, and my wife is unemployed, and so on ... so that these ... not only the Muslims are endangered here." Now at this point in time you have acknowledged that you knew that there had been at least two massacres of Muslims in Prijedor, one at Keraterm and one at Koricanske Stijene. You've acknowledged earlier today that you knew non-Serbs were being taken out of camps and murdered. And a moment ago you explained that it was an especially risky environment for Muslims. Now comparing the situation of Muslims in Prijedor to your own, your reduction in salary, your status as a subtenant, and your wife's employment status, and saying that "we are all endangered here," that is a deeply misleading and cynical comment of yours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to try to continue believing that you mean well and that you are seriously trying to understand the way I saw the situation and that I was not cynical or sarcastic. Maybe this was inappropriate, this comparison of salaries. You call me "mayor," although that's not a proper translation. I was the president of the local Assembly, and I would appreciate it if you would stop interpreting it that way. When I was going to work and coming back, I had to keep a document on me, a document issued by the Secretariat for National Defence, regarding work obligation. Without that document, any policeman, civilian or military, could have arrested me and sent me directly to the front. I had no time to say at all in this interview, but I want to tell you that several times I was intercepted by armed members of the Serbian police or army who had bloodshot eyes, maybe from drinking, I don't know, they would put a gun barrel through the windows of my car and say, "You keep driving around town here, having fun, while I have to fight," and it would all end in their trying to wheedle out some drink or cigarettes from me. I couldn't even report them. I didn't know their names. They did not have badges with names. They did not have anything on their uniforms. I could not identified them. I tried to report them but that's always the answer I got: If you don't know their names, then we can't do anything. Maybe this reference to my salary was not a good idea, but I did not ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, you said in your answer: "I had no time to say it all in this interview ..." Are you seriously contending that you failed to mention the fact that Muslims had been massacred by the police and the army in Prijedor in 1992, that they had been taken out of camps and killed because you didn't have enough time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for a reference? Where was it established that this was done by the army and the police? The man said nicely that individuals were taking out people.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was referring to the two massacres in the statements that were committed by the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, Mr. Stakic? Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Could the question please be repeated for me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. Dr. Stakic, in your earlier answer you said: "I had no time to say at all in this interview ..." And my question was: Are you seriously contending that that you failed to mention the fact that Muslims had been massacred by the police and army in Prijedor in 1992 and that they had been taken out of camps and killed because you didn't have enough time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, distinguished Prosecutor, I know that you were trained for this, and I am not an expert so I cannot judge how you're doing your job. I think you're doing it well. But you asked me about 60 marks and asked about the tenants. And I said here, in response to this journalist's concrete question, I could not tell him about all the things that I had experienced. That I did not feel safe. My life was not safe either. It wasn't only the Muslims. I'm not saying and I'm not trying to say that they were not more imperilled, but if you have that in the interview do find it and see what it was that I answered in respect of massacres. I am not trying to deny that. I'm not trying to diminish it. Really. Could you please -- well, I tried to answer the journalist's questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this interview, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6582, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 40633, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, this is a transcript of another video-recorded interview of you around the same time, January 1993, with a foreign journalist, where you are being asked primarily about the Geneva plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of this document in both languages. This is at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Where you're speaking, it says MS. And you're talking about the plan agreed to in Geneva, and you say: "And third, European monitors should come to the field to determine the factual state of affairs, so they don't make maps, projections, and constitutions based on the propaganda from Vatican and Tehran. One needs to come to Prijedor, see who lives here, who works, what they do, what their activities are, go to Krupa on Una, to Novi, to Sanski Most. I am talking about cities that are of interest here. To determine, to determine, to see what the situation really is, who lives here, and what they are doing. Then they should go away, take a week, and draw new maps." Now, here you are promoting the division of territory based on the factual situation on the ground at the time, based on who is actually living in Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, Krupa, and this would, of course, favour the Serbs given the drastic reduction in the Muslim and Croat population in these areas since the start of the war; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, I don't think -- I don't agree with you on this interpretation. First of all, as you can see, I'm supporting that agreement in Geneva; that is to say, that people accepted to talk in the first place. Which would mean that the war could be brought to an end by way of talks. Also, I do not mention in any way that Muslims and Croats should not live there. And finally, I don't know what year this was, this Geneva Agreement, but finally there was the Dayton Agreement. And it did bring about this final delineation into two entities. However, it did not say that only Serbs should live in the Serb entity; rather, the Muslims and Croats and everybody else should live there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is January 1993, and in January 1993, Dr. Stakic, there were very few Muslims and Croats in Prijedor and the other places you mention here, Krupa, Novi, Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were, but I did not say -- it's not written here anywhere that they should come and take that situation and that the people who had been expelled from there should not be allowed to return. I just welcomed and I wished that that agreement had been signed in 1993. As far as I know, the Serb side was in favour of that and not everybody was satisfied. To this day, not everybody is satisfied with the Dayton Agreement, but it is my profound belief that it is better. Any peace agreement is better than war. Also, in 1996, I had the opportunity of taking part in its implementation, especially paragraph 7, concerning the return of displaced persons to their properties. So if there was a delineation, and I said that I agree with the Geneva Agreement, that there should be a delineation, I did not say that a territory should be cleansed of a particular people.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you keep saying that you're just supporting the agreement in Geneva, but you're taking issue with maps based on propaganda from the Vatican and Tehran and you're asserting that those maps should be drawn on the factual situation based on who was living in these places now; right? You're making claims about the how the territory should be divided.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that it is written there now on the basis of the factual situation. Sorry, I really don't see that, at least not in the Serbian version. I'm saying that I agree that there should be this delineation and that all people should have the right to live at their homes, regardless of whether they are on this or that side of the line. And now I touched upon propaganda. It was coming from Belgrade, Sarajevo, Zagreb. Perhaps I went a bit too far there. After all, I was not in Dayton. But regarding what I learned, it's been almost 20 years now since Dayton. These maps were agreed upon and changed and altered. And finally when they were established, believe me, not a single side was fully satisfied with them. They all have their objections with regard to Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 in both languages, please. And this is near the middle of the page in English and about halfway down as well as in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So again, this is a lengthy passage where you're speaking, Dr. Stakic, and you say in the second line of that long answer you say: "Islam, i.e., jihad has won because a great number of Muslims from this region emigrated and went to Germany, i.e., the whole of Europe. Why do I mention this? Because all these Muslims from this region could have chosen to go to Zenica, Sarajevo, Travnik or Western Europe. They chose Western Europe and they wouldn't leave here. They wouldn't even hear Zenica mentioned or Travnik. They wouldn't even go to Croatia. They know they are not welcome there. On the contrary, they go to Europe, for economic reasons and the reasons preached to them by jihad." Now, again, Dr. Stakic, you knew at this point in time that Muslims had been massacred, that they had been taken out of camps and killed, and that this was an especially risky environment for non-Serbs. But you don't say any of this. You claim that Muslims left Prijedor during 1992 for economic reasons and the reasons preached to them by jihad. Again, you were trying to mislead this journalist about the real reasons for the Muslims leaving Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, I do not fully agree with your assertion. It is a fact that crimes were committed. It is a fact that they were expelled from their homes and thereby compelled to leave the area. However, you can find these documents that I'm aware of. I didn't bring them here because I didn't know about that. During my trial, at one point, either just when Trnopolje was being closed or after it had been closed, a new wave of civilians, Muslim civilians came to Trnopolje because they saw their chance there of leaving Prijedor. I agree with that part, that most of them left out of fear and so on and so forth, but what I'm saying here, where they were going and where they wanted to go, of course they wanted to go to Europe where there was no war rather than Croatia and Bosnia. Bosnia, the part under the control of the Croat forces, and they would be drafted into their army and they would have to fight there. And life was miserable there, too. And when I say jihad, Islam, that should not be equated. Part of them - how do I put this? - are extremists, like in any nation, and they obviously tried to profit from all of that, too. And I know from the experience of people who came to see me, and they were asking about -- about what was going on in either places. And from Bosanski Novi, a group of Muslims left in co-operation with the UNHCR. They were in Croatia at the time, Dvor na Uni - do you know the geography there? It's on the Una river - and through Croatia they went to Western Europe. And then a delegation came to see me, and they asked me how I could bring them into touch with these representatives of the UNHCR so that they do not go in the organisation of the Red Cross and others towards Zenica and Travnik. I am telling you about all of this from my very own experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, in your answer you said, "It is a fact that they were expelled from their homes and thereby compelled to leave the area." And you said, "I agree with that part that most of them left out of fear and so on and so forth ..." So when you said at paragraph 26 of your statement that "the main reason for moving out was the constant fighting, the lack of electric power, water, and basic food provisions," that's not true, is it, because you're acknowledging here that most of them left out of fear, that people were expelled and compelled to leave the area; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- even when I talked to the gentlemen from Mr. Karadzic's Defence, you know, we had this extensive discussion and then they would summarise my answer into a few sentences. I am not saying that they wrote anything that is not true, but they summarised. You see the next sentence here, "The war was no longer near the municipality. It was in the territory of the municipality itself." The very fact that there is a war going on. You know that. Who is safe in a war? Not to mention now what is going on in Syria. Somebody is rooting for one side and others are rooting for the other side, but it is civilians who are falling victim on both sides and from both sides. But in addition to that, there were economic reasons, a lack of electricity, water, food, and so on and so forth. But as I already mentioned, war was no longer only in the vicinity, in Krupa, in Croatia, and so on, but it was right there in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, this is simply my view. It occurred to me that if I was a person who had just come into the public gallery and listened to a good percentage of the questions, one might be mistaken that Dr. Stakic was the person who was on trial rather than Dr. Karadzic. I don't make this as a criticism of you, but I make it as an observation as to how much of this is really useful to the issues that are before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would respond with two points. Firstly, I think a lot of this goes to credibility. The second point would be that, in the indictment -- I mean, Dr. Stakic plays a role in the indictment either as a tool or as a member of the JCE. He's obviously connected to Dr. Karadzic through his position, and I would leave it at that. I'm about to move on to another topic in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's much easier to observe a cross-examination than it is to do one. I've been in that position many a time myself in the past. But it seems to me that the two issues that you raise, that of credibility and joint enterprise, could be dealt with in a much smaller compass.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, at paragraph 14 you said that the Prijedor municipal authorities had no contact or communication with the Pale authorities until the corridor breakthrough. And I'd like you to clarify when this communication blockade began according to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say what the date was exactly, but it was sometime in the month of May, when the joint forces of the Croats and Muslims severed the road going from Banja Luka to Bijeljina and thereby to the Republic of Serbia. I really do apologise. I cannot tell you what the exact date would be, but I think it was the month of May. And then up until the end of June, the beginning of July, to the best of my knowledge, when the Army of Republika Srpska managed to liberate the road or the corridor, as they called it, thereby -- I mean, in my view and to the best of my knowledge, telephone lines were reestablished because we could speak to Belgrade. And also, the power supply was somewhat improved. Also, vehicles started moving along and --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I said there that we, the municipal authorities, did not have any communication, that I did not have any communication. Because the paragraph says further on whether the police and the army were able to communicate, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I thank you. And again, I'd like to ask you to please focus to the precise question I asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P3537, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to 65 ter 40633, the interview, is that going to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, I do tender that, the first -- the part of the interview that relates to Dr. Stakic. I think it's the first four pages in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6583, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first part, not including Penny Marshall part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, the first four pages which -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What -- are we admitting only -- the only page that was shown to the witness? Four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think there were multiple pages shown to the witness but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- there's only four pages in which he's being interviewed and then the next two pages of the English transcript involves someone else's interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. As in the previous case, we will admit them all. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, this is in 22nd of May, 1992, Prijedor Crisis Staff decision on mobilisation, and you can see in the preamble it says: "Pursuant to the decision of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the general public mobilisation of forces and materiel in the republic." And indeed, the Chamber has received in evidence a Presidency mobilisation decision from the 20th of May; that's P3919. So I take it that whatever communication difficulties you had, you did receive the republic level decision on mobilisation as indicated in this decision; right? On the -- in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honoured Prosecutor, to the best of my recollection, general mobilisation -- well, if I'm not talking about the one at the level of the former Yugoslavia that was in 1991. General mobilisation was declared by the Republika Srpska or the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whatever it was called, in the month of April, if I'm not mistaken. And we are just invoking that decision. As I said a moment ago, we could not forbid anything. We are appealing to the citizenry to respond to this decision that had already been made at a higher level and that is compulsory for all citizens, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P3919, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we see that document, can we go into private session briefly. Yes. We can upload the document in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, here you can see the decision issued by Dr. Karadzic as president of the Presidency on general public mobilisation of forces and resources in the republic, dated the 20th of May, 1992. A moment ago, you said that to the best of your recollection, the general mobilisation was declared by the Republika Srpska in the month of April. Now, does this remind you of the general mobilisation decision issued by the Presidency just two days before the Prijedor Crisis Staff issued its mobilisation decision?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen this decision at all. And there is no reason to have this sent to me, as president of the Municipal Assembly. I really do not recall having seen this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we can go back to P3537.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 39, in discussing adjudicated fact 1029, you state that the Prijedor Crisis Staff met for the first time on the 29th of May, 1992, and you repeated that claim today in your testimony. Now, if you could look again at the preamble of this 22nd of May Crisis Staff decision, it states that this decision was reached at the meeting held on the 22nd of May. So in fact, the Prijedor Crisis Staff did meet before the 29th of May, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can this be moved a bit up? It does say the Crisis Staff here, and the date is 22nd May. However, earlier I claimed that there were no sessions before the 29th of May. Why did I claim that? If you look at the minutes of the Assembly sessions that were recorded from July or August 1992, where all the decisions of the Crisis Staff were adopted, and those decisions were made between 22 May and 17 July. So this may be a mistake. Maybe it was the Council for National Defence, and maybe it was mistyped as the Crisis Staff. This is just my assumption. You know that if this was a Crisis Staff meeting, then this decision would have made it to all the collective decisions of the Crisis Staff. There would have been a document containing all the decisions of the Crisis Staff including this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 10949, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, this again is from the 25th of September, 1992, issue of "Kozarski Vjesnik," and the article I'd like to direct you to is the one in the middle and of the top of the page, "Milicija nije vojska," and the article describes a meeting held on the 18th of September, 1992, with policemen who had returned from Han Pijesak with the municipal authorities, including you. Now, without getting into the details of that meeting at the moment, do you remember holding this meeting with the policemen who had returned from Han Pijesak around this time, mid-September 1992, to address a series of demands that they were making?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date but I do remember the meeting. It happened before, soldiers or police members would deflect [as interpreted] from the front line, but this was a bigger group which is why I remembered this event. I don't know if it was an entire unit, but it was a large group in any case, which is why I remember the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if I could direct your attention to the very bottom of the left-hand column of this article. And this is at the very bottom -- it starts at the very bottom of the page in the English and moves onto the next page, and it says -- it's referring to the sixth demand of the police members. It says: "In their sixth demand," and if we could turn the page in the English, "the policemen wanted to know why the prisoners from Keraterm, Omarska and Trnopolje had been released. Stakic indicated the two key reasons which had motivated the government in Pale to make such a decision: Pressure from international public opinion and official policy, and the steep cost of maintaining the prisons." Now it's correct, is it not, as this article indicates, that the decision to close down Omarska and Keraterm was made by the government in Pale, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this decision, but I did see and I heard that a decision was made by the Ministry of the Interior to close them down. Simo Drljaca kept on repeating that he couldn't do that and that he received promises from the army that they would open another prison or a reception centre, as they were called, so a prison was opened in Manjaca. And as a result of that, there were no longer reasons to keep the other two open and to keep the people there. Those who were found to be guilty of war crimes could be transferred to Manjaca and the others were released. This is what I know. I can't claim that I saw a decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could tender this article and move on to 65 ter 18416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6584, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And does the Chamber wish to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 20 minutes and resume at five past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if I could have 65 ter 18416, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Stakic, you can see that this is a 22nd of August, 1992, "Srna" press release titled: "Investigating centre in Omarska abolished." And it states that: "The government authorities in Prijedor inform that the investigating centre in Omarska had been closed down in the course of the day, and the open camp in Trnopolje given to the authority of the Red Cross, according to the decision of the Presidency of Republika Srpska." Now, just before the break you said that you had heard that the minister of the interior made a decision to close down Omarska and Keraterm. Does this press release remind you that this was in fact a Presidency decision?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this is what I can read here. I can't, however, say that this is correct or not. Whoever drafted this and signed it could perhaps tell you what the news is based on. I apologise, I can't tell you. I can read as well as you, but I can't confirm that this is true because I never saw a decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Who informed you that it was the -- that the decision to close down Omarska and Keraterm came from the Pale authorities? How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca said that finally a camp was open in Manjaca for prisoners of war. From the very beginning, he claimed that an institution of that kind should be run by the military, not by the police, and that finally that institution was opened, and that as a result of that, the centres would be closed down, and that the prisoners who, according to them, were guilty of a crime, would be transferred to Manjaca. I don't know who he received that information from, whether it was from his own minister or from somebody else. I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this press release says that during the course of that day, which was the 22nd of August, Omarska had been closed down and that Trnopolje had been handed over to the authority of the Red Cross. And is that information consistent with your knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, with all due respect. However, it was about that time in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this news release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Stakic, in the course of your meetings with the Karadzic Defence or with your own attorney, did you become aware that Dr. Karadzic has presented evidence in his defence that it was the Prijedor Crisis Staff that was responsible for the mass killings of non-Serbs, the destruction of their homes, and the drastic reduction of the non-Serb population in 1992? And I refer to D2265, page 59, as well as pages 50, 56, and 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. This may be a technical objection but it is of some importance, and that is that I don't believe that any conversations he had with his own attorney is something that should be within the scope of her question as it would be privileged.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I can just ask the question generally.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you learn that information, Dr. Stakic, that Dr. Karadzic has presented evidence in his defence that it's the Prijedor Crisis Staff that's responsible for all the crimes against non-Serbs in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that. This is the first time I hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor please call up the document and could she refrain from asking questions without showing him corroborating documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's for the purpose of reference to the parties, for the benefit of the parties. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now you agreed at the outset of your testimony that the police and army committed mass crime against Muslims and Croats in Prijedor in 1992, detention, torture, killings, et cetera, and that was at page 24. And you made clear your position that you were not a big player or the main player. And that was also at page 24. Now, you would agree, I take it, that Dr. Karadzic, the president and Supreme Commander, had far greater authority over the police and the army than you, president of the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect to you and this Tribunal, I don't think that I am the right person to qualify him as the person most responsible for everything. I'm here as a witness, albeit a Defence witness. However, I'm here to give the Trial Chamber my own view of the situation at the time in order to help the Trial Chamber shed light on the developments. I believe that Mr. Karadzic has a good Defence team and that they will help him defend himself. If I mentioned the military and the police here, I meant the local forces. I know that there was a hierarchy, a vertical hierarchy and that they were duty-bound to report to their superiors according to that vertical hierarchy. What reports they sent, how they sent them, I wouldn't know, but -- because that information reached me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stakic. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am sorry. I wanted one page and I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Stakic, on page 73 of today's transcript, it was suggested that you were a member of the joint criminal enterprise together with me. Were you with me in a joint criminal enterprise of any kind --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. That was not a question to the witness. It's perfectly clear I was responding to a comment from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it's perfectly plain that that was an answer from Ms. Gustafson to the query that I raised. It was not a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I apologise. But the way I see it, the Prosecutor doesn't do anything without a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On pages 71 and 72, it was suggested that you should accept that Muslims and Croats were expelled and forced to leave from Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, again, those were the witness's words. It wasn't put to him that he should accept that. Let's just make sure we're not mischaracterising his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, were Muslims and Croats expelled? Were they forced to leave? If that was the case, who did that? What forced them to leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already stated, both in my statement and earlier today in the course of my testimony, which is recorded on the transcript, as war approached Prijedor and when war operations started in earnest in the municipality of Prijedor, and as I have repeated several times here, as a result of that the rate of crime went up, there was looting, theft, and people started moving out of their houses. Not all of them but a lot of them did. Temporarily, they were accommodated in Trnopolje, and then later, with the help of the Red Cross, they went to some other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and further afield. Further afield. One more thing that I didn't say here and now it has just occurred to me, I remember that I saw certain documents issued by the Ministry of Health, if I'm not mistaken. They were signed by Dr. Kalinic, and I don't know what his position was at the time, but I know that together with the Muslim and Croatian representatives he signed a document on the free movement of the civilian population, which meant that they were free to cross from one side of the front line to the other side. I would like to add that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lines 1, 2, and 3 on page 72. It says clearly: [In English] "... that's not true, is it, because you are acknowledging here that most of them left out of fear, that people were expelled and compelled to leave the area; right?" [Interpretation] I'm asking you, Dr. Stakic, did somebody go to their homes? Did somebody force them to leave their homes? Or was it indeed the case this they were afraid and that's why they fled? Just like you told us? What you said in paragraph 26 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic, that's a leading question, very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they were expelled like it was suggested and that they were forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, not only is it leading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- but Dr. Karadzic was reading from my follow-up question, which referred back to the witness's assertion that this is exactly what happened. So this whole exercise is misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may refer to his answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will move on and then I'll see what I'm going to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 66, it was suggested that you accepted the fact that the police and the army committed massacres. You were aware that there were killings and that there was, indeed, a massacre, or rather, a mass killing in Keraterm and another one at Koricanske Stijene. Did you accept the fact that it had been planned by the military and the police; or if not, did you know who did that? If you agree that this was a planned effort by the military and the police, then the answer is yes; but if not, can you tell us who did it and how?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I start answering or should I wait?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that I answered that I was aware of the fact that massacres indeed took place, but the Prosecutor did not have any follow-up questions. But now I can answer your question. When I say the police and the military, I mean that in these two specific cases I had my views or, rather, I had information that was conveyed to me. As for the killings of those wretched people in Keraterm, it was the local battalion and reservists who were responsible for those. Allegedly, they did it because several Serbian soldiers were killed at the front line and in retaliation they burst into Keraterm and killed those innocent people. Neither then nor now have I heard that it was organised by the command of those troops or somebody else of that kind. I even heard that Mr. Drljaca said, because he was angry and because there were police officers who were supposed to guard those people and those men wanted to take it on the police, so Mr. Drljaca said that he would take it up with the army. I don't know what happened next because I don't have any information to that effect. And the next big shame inflicted not only upon me and the Serbs from Prijedor but the entire Serbian population was the case of Koricanske Stijene. I repeat once again, those people from Trnopolje were allowed to link up with their families. It was the Red Cross that enabled them to do that. And the police and the military were supposed to make arrangements with this other side to open the passage for the convoy of buses. Those policemen, and it is not up to me to be the judge of them, but I can say that they were not humans because not only did they rob those poor people but they also executed them. I condemn that as a human being, as a person. I'd like to say this: I'm not Mr. Drljaca's advocate. I don't want to defend him. We were at odds at times because he had a strong personality. Sometimes he was harsh in his comport. But when I learned about that event I called him about a document because, you know, us civilians had to have an approval from the military district and from the police to pass through that corridor. So I called him and he was in a very bad mood, and he said: Now you call me when my police officers had done something really, really unprecedentedly stupid. I'll call you later. So what I'm saying is that I wouldn't say that somebody had a plan to do that. At least I wasn't aware of any such plan. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about investigation centres and a reference was made to Omarska and so on and so forth. You were asked about the civilian authorities that set it up. Can you tell me how come that your police did not carry out investigations in the detention unit that existed in the public security station?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand your question. Why didn't the police do what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was mis-recorded and this was misinterpreted. What I wanted to say is this: The last document says that Omarska was an investigation centre. I'm asking you this: If Omarska was an investigation centre and if all the investigations were carried out there, how come that the police did not detain people in their own existing detention unit which existed in the police station?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. The question assumes that there were no detentions and investigations at the Prijedor police station. I don't have any -- I don't have the evidence at my fingertips, but I am quite sure that that is not the case. So the question, I think, should be rephrased or a preliminary question asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that you can reformulate your question. I didn't follow it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, was there a detention unit attached to the MUP in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes. But I don't know. I don't know for how many people, five, six, ten, not more than that, because local criminals and drunkards would be detained there temporarily and then they would be taken to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, Dr. Karadzic, and Your Honours, either because of what I have on my ears and I also hear the spoken word, I heard "your police" a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Prijedor police.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that that was just a slip of the tongue on your part, but please, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. The size of this detention unit, does it have anything to do with using Omarska for investigations?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I cannot say anything unequivocally here because, as I've already said, that's not my line of work. But knowing that in Omarska there were many more people -- I saw during the trial that 3.000 people went through Omarska. That figure is telling enough. And knowing that this detention unit could take only five or six people, on the basis of that, I can conclude -- infer, rather - it's deduction, isn't it? - that it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked or, rather, it was established, it was stated that Muslims and Croats lived in a risky environment. That's on page 55. Can you tell us when this environment became risky in terms of dates?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me, Your Honours, I remember in my case it was repeated time and again that on the 1st of May different campaigns started, killings, that there was a lack of safety and security and so on. I would say now that only after Hambarine on the 20th of May, especially Kozarac, the 24th of May, when the Muslim extremists dared attack the army, thereby entering a direct conflict with the army, then there was fighting. And then after that, this true situation of war and crisis and fear and everything else started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 3, I believe you said on the 22nd of May rather than the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And on the 24th Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why it did not become dangerous already on the 6th of April as it became in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We still had a joint Assembly that was established on the basis of the interparty agreement at the republican level reached between the HDZ and the SDS. It was violated, to the best of my knowledge, in autumn 1991 when the SDA and HDZ MPs outvoted the SDS and they left the Assembly. We continued to work together on local levels. Because you know what it's like, the houses are mixed. There were hardly any hamlets that were purely Muslim or purely Serb, and especially the population in town itself. And you can see that from the transcripts of the joint Assembly. We tried to keep it together. We didn't succeed, but we called upon Muslim assemblymen from the SDA, saying that we should reach an agreement at local level in order to share power, all with a view to preserving the peace. Although -- well, you mentioned Sarajevo, but I would like to mention municipalities that are closer to Prijedor. It already started in Bosanska Krupa and Sanski Most, in April, also, to the best of my recollection. And in Prijedor there was no war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also you were asked and you gave an answer. You said the Muslims could go to Central Bosnia and that they could go to Germany. Did the Muslims have an opportunity to stay on in Prijedor itself? Were there agreements about the transformation of Prijedor where they would exercise authority over themselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could just specify the time-period with this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, was it only Central Bosnia and Germany or did they have a third option, Prijedor itself?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could stay in Prijedor and a number of them did stay on throughout the war. Truth to tell we are dealing with 1992 here, but I would like to say something. A large number, I don't know exactly how many, Muslims left in 1995 when -- how do I put this? When there was this major influx of Serbs, the Serb population from the Krajina that was flooding in. Also, they could establish their own municipality and declare their own territory, and then also even after the take-over of power on the 1st of May, and that can be seen from documents. There was a mixed police force as well, and they were told they could take part in this local commune. And in Kozarac the entire police stayed on. And there were no problems whatsoever all the way up until the 24th of May. That is to say, I agree they did have that option. In those areas where they were the majority population, they could stay on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript does not say Ljubija and that's the location. You mentioned it together with Kozarac; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ljubija, Kozarac, that's what I mentioned, two enclaves. And they're not small, between 10- and 12.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested to you that you spoke about the life of Muslims in Prijedor and that already by the end of 1992 there were very few Muslims left. Can you tell us how come this happened then, that I was pressured in the autumn of 1994 to release 80 trucks full of Muslims per day and that they stayed on, and how come there were thousands of Muslims left in 1994, and by the end of 1995 there were several thousand --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- Muslims in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- this is all leading. It hasn't been established that the witness knows anything about these assertions about trucks and thousands of Muslims in 1994. Those foundational questions have to be asked before these ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you rephrase your question? Otherwise, we need to go back to the page where he spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm sorry. I'm going to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that you spoke to journalists about the life of Muslims in Prijedor, although you knew that then, at the end of 1992, there were very few Muslims left in Prijedor. Is that correct, that at the end of 1992 there were very few Muslims left in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said to the Prosecutor that there was no official census at the time, but I would like to repeat what I said a moment ago; that is that when the Dayton Agreement was signed - that is to say, in December 1995 - there were still some Muslims in Prijedor. And I mentioned a moment ago as well that when tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands, Serb refugees, came to Prijedor and went through Prijedor, quite a few Muslims also left Prijedor. That's the period of August and September 1995. And I still claim that a number of them stayed on. I cannot say exactly what the numbers involved are or the percentage, but I do know some people who lived there, worked there, I saw them in the building and they were in town. The population was mixed. Cela, Donji Jakupovici, those were Muslims neighbourhoods. And these enclaves -- people from these enclaves did not move out at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there Muslims and Croats on our police force?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes. As for exact numbers, I wouldn't know, but there were some. That can be checked, too. In the veterans organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, generally speaking, what did this depend on; namely, that some Muslims could stay and others felt threatened or were detained or interrogated or were just leaving Prijedor? What was decisive in that respect? Your will, the will of your local authorities and the army and the police to group Muslims or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're just losing your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And not stopping with a non-leading question and having to add -- add to the question that makes it leading, it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as briefly as possible: How come some of them could stay on and others could not? If the systemic approach was that the Muslims should disappear, how come some can stay and others do not stay. It is a perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Let's go back to the part which was dealt with and start from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the beginning is there. The Prosecutor suggested that Dr. Stakic deceived the journalist, speaking about the life of Muslims in Prijedor although he knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then upload that document and ask your question based upon the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the document is now, but I know that it's in the transcript, that it was put to him that I intentionally misled or deceived the journalist. But I'm going to abandon the topic in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, on page 51, yet again it was discussed whether you could issue orders to the army or the police. Even if you did send an order to the army or the police, what would happen to that kind of order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that you've put that question, I'll answer by telling you about something that I experienced in 1993 when I was no longer president and when I was replaced by another gentleman, and I did have some objections.
