The local committee of the party was objecting, actually. They said that I am not influencing the army and the police sufficiently. They actually wanted to have all assemblymen and all members of the SDS freed of military obligation and military duty, and I said we cannot do that. We can pass an Assembly decision, but they don't have to observe that. Now I'm going back to what I was saying, when this new president came from that stream, that is to say, these people who thought that they could -- or, rather, that I as president could have issued orders. I and the late Dr. Kovacevic were sitting there. We had a colleague from Belgrade who had come to perform some operations on some children so that we wouldn't have to take them there. So it so happened that Mr. Pero Colic, commander of the Prijedor Brigade, entered that restaurant and said, "Look at the document that I got a few days ago from the president of the municipality, where he says, 'I, president of the municipality, hereby order Pero Colic ..." and so on and so forth," and this man says I was wondering whether I should send the military police to arrest him and take him to the front. But what prevailed was that we shouldn't heighten tensions any further, so I gave up. Who does this man think he is? Well, so much for that. That's what it would have meant, if I even did write an order to him. I hope I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 42 it was suggested to you that the Crisis Staff decided who would be released but not the way in which they would be released. Could you tell us you did not allow these group releases? What's the distinction between individual releases and group releases?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain that but I'll try to once again. The police were assuring us, at least, and perhaps you'll see that, too. They got all these lawyers busy, 40, 60 lawyers from their services, from the court and I don't know from what other places. And they were interrogating these detained persons, and they decided who was guilty and who was not guilty, who would be sent to Trnopolje and who would be released. Now, what was it that made us try to intervene? Precisely that, that Serb criminals decided to enter these centres. And I don't know how they did it there. Were they in cahoots with the guards or did they deceive them, but they took people out. It wasn't groups. They would go there and ask for particular individuals by name and surname, and they said that they would return them, that they just needed to reach some kind of agreement. Usually it had to do with extortion, to get money from them or immovable property, if they had any. And the most regrettable thing was that afterwards they would kill these people. After this kind of knowledge, after we heard about this, we tried to appeal to the police to prevent that kind of thing from happening and not allowing such individuals to enter such centres in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was also suggested to you on page 33 or perhaps 34 that the Muslim population in "celina" was attacked, and mention was also made of Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 20209. And the reference for what I said about the journalist is page 17, lines 13 through 18.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Page 70, seventy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the texts has been translated. Can we get the English translation. This is dealing with the consequences of the attack or removing the consequences of attack. Yes. This is it. Everybody can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you to look at the very short text in the upper right-hand side corner. Apologies, this is on the 5th of June, 1995 [as interpreted]. What does it say on the upper right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you zoom in on that part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Attackers came from Stari Grad. Do you me to read just this or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe you could give us your own summary.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 4.30 this morning, members of Muslim paramilitary formations carried out an attack from various directions and from various areas, and in particular from the direction of Stari Grad, Pecani, and Tukova --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they attacked the facilities of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, the police station, Prijedor hotel, the city bridge on the Sana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you accepted the Prosecutor's suggestion that the population in "celina" in Stari Grad was attacked?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not describe it that way. I tried to answer the Prosecutor's question by answering why they hadn't crossed the bridge on the Sana, because there is only one bridge on the Sana that was opened at the moment because it was secure. There was a police and military check-point there. And as for the Prijedor hotel, where one part of that unit was billeted, they didn't go from there. They went down the stream of the Sana and they arrived in the centre. When they were withdrawing, they took the same route, whereas the troops followed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few interventions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's purely my personal observation, but I find it strange that you base your questions in your re-examination on the question put by the Prosecutor during her cross-examination, not on the answers given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I could just add, Your Honour, that the question was "whether you accepted the Prosecutor's suggestion that the population in 'celina' in Stari Grad was attacked." What I put to him was that after the attacking force was repelled, the army destroyed the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So it's also not an accurate characterisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, the witnesses are used to our system, and they cannot be mindful of the tricks in the questions, and I cannot intervene during the cross-examination and that's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Celina" is not a place. "Celina" is the word for entire population. It's not a place. It's not a location. So when a witness confirms something without this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did say you're very skillful in what you do because he sensed that the questions were tricky. Okay. Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Totally inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is inappropriate is the fact that we are being tried in such a system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see the removal of consequences through a glance and tell us whether this is corresponds to what you knew about the situation at the time. This document or, rather, this text.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, just look at it. Could we look at the very short paragraph: At the meeting of the Crisis Staff, problems of the temporarily resettled population was considered after they took refuge in some of the camps in order to save [indiscernible] from war operations? What camp did the author have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that he had in mind Trnopolje because Keraterm and Omarska were places where people were put to be investigated after having been arrested during combat. And as for Trnopolje, as I've already told you, people would go there to seek shelter. And then when the Red Cross started organising their departure, it was allowed for the people to join their families up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the meaning of the term "those who moved out temporarily"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered a question to that effect. The document was signed by all the three parties, and in that document there was a reference to temporarily moving out during the war while the population was in danger as a result of war operations, and I personally accepted that. And I thought once some day when peace was restored, that all those who wanted to return would be able to return to their homes. And this is indeed what is happening, what is still happening, in accordance with the Dayton Accords, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender this document but we would also request the part on Stari Grad to be translated, the part that Dr. Stakic started reading out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am not sure which part you made Mr. Stakic read out in addition to those that have been already translated. Shall we mark it for identification, pending English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI D4203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to put on the record now that I'm not sure exactly what Dr. Karadzic is referring to. I may have objections when this is translated because at this point I just can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's the purpose of marking for identification. Do you have more questions, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will finish on time, your Excellencies. I have a few short questions. Can this entire document be tendered? We would like to have all the text because they could be of much help to the Trial Chamber if Dr. Stakic confirms that that is what indeed happened at the time and that "Kozarski Vjesnik" accurately conveyed news of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, we did not meddle with the editorial policy of "Kozarski Vjesnik," and now you have not given me an opportunity to read all that. However, the parts that I read, I can agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at first there was no communication but you still managed to receive certain instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind the participants of the fact that P02716 on page 22 says that during the first 45 days, we did not have any contacts, and this is from a meeting with the leadership of Prijedor. We can call it up if you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If he wants to call up a document, that's fine. But this preliminary exposition on what the document says is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document has been admitted. I'm just asking the doctor whether it is true whether there were to contacts and whether that corresponds to what he experienced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said to the -- I apologise to everybody and to the interpreters. Can I be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What? I don't remember what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The question appears to have been based on P2716, so I think as an initial step that should be called up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So before we see the document, what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked Dr. Stakic, since during cross-examination his contention that there had been no contacts was challenged and some instructions were shown, I am now asking Dr. Stakic, considering that at that first meeting we had noted that there had been no meetings, that was page 2716 -- that was P2716, page 22. I am asking him now if that's consistent with what he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. I answered the same to the lady from the Prosecution. Although, I didn't have the exact number of days that we hadn't seen each other. I don't know exactly how soon the corridor was closed. But I know that I had no contact with you, personally. Nor did the others, I believe, because we in Bosnian Krajina were not able to reach anyone outside by phone. And I also added that I don't know whether the army or the police had some communications of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question. Evidence was led in the form of evidence of Witness Srdjo Srdic in 2002 that it was the Crisis Staff that organised it all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the last part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. Could you repeat your last sentence again for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask Dr. Stakic -- I cannot show this document of three or four passages that the Prosecution cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking how old he was, Srdjo Srdic, in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR STAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think over 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I cannot clear that up now because we have no time. Thank you, Dr. Stakic, for coming here and for your evidence. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stakic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I thank the ladies and gentlemen of the Prosecution and Mr. Karadzic and his Defence team. I hope that I managed to give some contribution at least to your efforts to shed light on the events of 1992. It's up to you, of course. Thank you and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our thanks also go to Mr. Ostojic for your assistance. Thank you very much. I appreciate it. And I also appreciate the kind indulgence of the staff and the interpreters and everybody involved. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of December, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
